abstract: |
  The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism measures embodied carbon plant by plant and cuts the charge only by carbon prices effectively paid. Both rules undermine its second purpose, encouraging trading partners to decarbonize. A producer with blast furnaces and scrap-fed electric furnaces can send scrap-based steel to Europe and sell the rest elsewhere; in a stylized case the charge falls by three quarters while emissions do not change. And a revenue-neutral feebate, which charges every producer the full rate at the margin, earns nothing because its average payment is zero. I show that measuring embodied carbon and the foreign price signal by country and sector removes the gain from shuffling and rewards the feebate, propose a liability formula, and calibrate it to the EU's default values. At €80 per tonne of carbon dioxide, routing scrap-based steel to Europe saves €100–600 per tonne. Recognizing the signal halves the export share at which a feebate pays for itself.

*Working paper, version 0.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Legal texts are as of 29 October 2026. A short version is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.3 [@CFPB13]; version 0.2 was the author's submission to the Commission's consultation of May–June 2026 [@Stretton2026Submission]. All CBAM amounts are in euros.*

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is the first border charge on embodied carbon at scale, and its design choices will shape which carbon-pricing instruments its trading partners adopt. Since January 2026 importers of iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity have owed certificates for the emissions embodied in what they import, priced in line with the EU Emissions Trading System and on sale from February 2027, while free allocation to EU producers phases out by 2034 [@EU2023; @EU2025Omnibus]. At €80 per tonne of carbon dioxide and full phase-in, the charge on a tonne of hot-rolled steel from India, declared at the Commission's default value with its 30 percent mark-up, is €445; from China, €331; from Türkiye, €252 (@sec-calibration).

The mechanism has two purposes. The first is a level playing field: an imported tonne of steel should bear the same carbon cost as a tonne made in the EU, and no tonne should be charged twice. The second is to encourage the countries that export to Europe to decarbonize their own production. Two rules serve the first purpose well and the second badly. Embodied carbon is measured plant by plant, from verified installation data or from a country default value. And the charge falls only by a carbon price "effectively paid" in the country of production, net of "any rebate or other form of compensation" [@EU2025Omnibus, Art. 9(1)].

Each rule creates a flaw. Plant-level measurement lets an exporter with both blast furnaces and scrap-based electric arc furnaces route the scrap-based steel to Europe and the rest elsewhere, cutting the carbon the border sees without cutting the carbon in the atmosphere. Price-paid recognition credits payments, not incentives: a revenue-neutral feebate charges every producer the full rate on each tonne above a sector benchmark and rebates the rest, so it sends the full price signal while its average producer pays nothing. The Commission's draft rules on the carbon price paid treat emissions "below an emission intensity baseline" as compensation to be netted off [@EU2026DraftCarbonPrice, Art. 8(1)(b)(ii)], so the feebate earns nothing. The instrument most likely to survive the politics of a large emitter, because it returns its revenue, is the one CBAM ignores.

The question this paper answers is how CBAM should measure embodied carbon and foreign carbon prices so that it rewards decarbonization rather than routing. The answer is to measure the foreign *price signal*, the marginal cost a country's instruments put on emitting, by country and sector, and to credit it alongside the price paid. Country-sector measurement does not depend on which plant shipped the goods, so routing earns nothing. A domestic feebate prices every tonne the country makes, not only the tenth that reaches Europe, so crediting it buys decarbonization of the whole sector. The Total Effective Carbon Price of paper 1.7 [@CFPB17] supplies the measure, for price and non-price instruments alike.

The paper makes four contributions.

1. **A model of route shuffling** (@sec-shuffling). Under plant-level measurement an exporter sends its low-carbon output to the EU up to its capacity or its EU sales, whichever binds, and its CBAM bill falls by $\tau(e_B - e_S)$ per tonne routed, with no change in its emissions (Proposition 1). When scrap is scarce, world emissions do not change either: the reported cut is relabeling (Proposition 2). Under country-sector measurement the bill does not depend on routing, but the incentive each plant faces is diluted by the EU's share of sales (Proposition 3). No empirical study of shuffling in steel exists; the evidence is from electricity.
2. **A liability formula** (@sec-recognition). A feebate earns nothing under price-paid recognition (Proposition 4). I propose that certificates be surrendered on $(\tau - r)^{+}$ per tonne of embodied carbon measured at the country-sector average, where the recognized price $r$ adds a weight $\rho$ on the unpaid part of the price signal. The liability is invariant to shuffling, and with full recognition each exporter's most competitive feebate rate equals the EU's carbon price, as in Proposition 7 of the companion paper on open-economy carbon pricing [@StrettonWP11] (Proposition 5).
3. **The verification trade-off** (@sec-tradeoff). Any rule that rewards a plant for verifying its own low intensity also rewards shipping from the cleanest plant, one for one (Proposition 6). I recommend a hybrid: country-sector measurement for countries with a recognized price signal, which then supplies the plant-level incentive itself, and firm-level verification of whole output for the rest.
4. **A calibration** (@sec-calibration) to the Commission's published default values for 119 countries. The shuffling gain is €100–600 per tonne of steel routed. Full recognition halves the share of a sector's output that must go to the EU before a feebate at the EU price pays for itself, from one half to about a quarter.

The paper belongs to a series. Paper 1.1 sets out the two-track architecture, a production feebate and a destination-based consumption charge, and proves that a charge on embodied carbon makes each exporter's most competitive feebate rate equal to the charge [@StrettonWP11]. Paper 1.2 designs feebates [@CFPB12]; paper 1.7 measures any instrument as a carbon-price equivalent [@CFPB17]. This paper applies them to the border mechanism that exists.

# CBAM as legislated {#sec-law}

**CBAM rests on two measurements, and both are plant-level by default.** The importer surrenders certificates equal to the embodied emissions of its imports, adjusted for the free allocation EU producers still receive, less a reduction for carbon prices paid abroad [@EU2023]. Embodied emissions are declared either from actual values, verified by an accredited verifier at the installation, or from default values set by the Commission [@EU2023, Art. 7; @EU2025Methods; @EU2025Verification]. For iron and steel and aluminum only direct emissions count; the default-value tables report no indirect values for them [@EU2025Defaults]. @tbl-legal lists the texts and their status.

| Text | Subject | Status at 29 October 2026 |

| Regulation (EU) 2023/956 | Establishes CBAM; definitive period from 1 January 2026; free allocation phased out by 2034 | In force; Article 9 replaced by 2025/2083 |
| Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 | Simplification: 50-tonne threshold; new Article 9 with yearly default carbon prices; default values at country averages plus mark-up (Annex IV, point 4.1) | In force since October 2025 |
| Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 | Default values by country and product, with mark-ups | Applies from 1 January 2026; revision due by December 2027 |
| Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2620 | Free-allocation adjustment, with benchmarks by production route | In force |
| Implementing Regulations (EU) 2025/2546 and 2025/2547 | Verification principles; methods for calculating embedded emissions | In force |
| Draft implementing regulation, Ares(2026)4841230 | Carbon price paid in a third country: conversion, evidence, independent persons | Feedback 13 May–10 June 2026 (177 responses); not adopted |
| COM(2025) 989 | Proposal: downstream goods, anti-circumvention, pre-consumer scrap | Pending in co-decision |
| COM(2025) 783 | Commission report on the application of CBAM | Published December 2025 |

: Legal texts on CBAM carbon price recognition and embodied emissions. Status from the EU Publications Office index and the Commission's Have Your Say portal, 29 October 2026. Appendix C gives references and the full list. Sources: @EU2023, @EU2025Omnibus, @EU2025Defaults, @EU2025FreeAllocation, @EU2025Verification, @EU2025Methods, @EU2026DraftCarbonPrice, @EU2025Downstream, @EU2025Review. {#tbl-legal}

**Default values are country averages with a penalty on top.** Since the 2025 amendment, default values "shall be set at the average emission intensity of each exporting country ... increased by a proportionately designed mark-up"; where reliable country data are lacking, at the average of the ten exporting countries with the highest intensities [@EU2025Omnibus, Annex IV point 4.1, recital 35]. Implementing Regulation 2025/2621 sets the mark-up for iron and steel, aluminum and cement at 10 percent in 2026, 20 percent in 2027 and 30 percent from 2028, and 1 percent for fertilizers [@EU2025Defaults]. For hot-rolled flat steel (CN 7208), the defaults before mark-up are 4.28 tCO₂ per tonne for India, 3.19 for China and 2.43 for Türkiye, and 4.05 for countries without reliable data. Each country line also carries a production-route code that sets the benchmark for the free-allocation adjustment [@EU2025FreeAllocation]. The mark-up has a job: a plant cleaner than its marked-up country default gains by filing verified data, so the mark-up draws data out of the cleaner half of plants. A plant dirtier than the default has no reason to file.

**Article 9 credits payments, and only where a carbon price is set by rule.** Under Article 9(1), as replaced in 2025, a declarant using actual emissions may claim a reduction "only if the carbon price has been effectively paid", and "any rebate or other form of compensation available in that country that would have resulted in a reduction of that carbon price shall be taken into account" [@EU2025Omnibus]. A declarant using default values may claim a reduction only by reference to yearly default carbon prices, and only "where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country" (Art. 9(4)). The Commission "may", "as from 2027", "for third countries where carbon pricing rules are in place, determine and make available ... the default carbon prices for those third countries and publish the methodology for their calculation", using "the best available data", "including on a conservative basis" (Art. 9(4); recital 20). Article 9(5) empowers the Commission to set by implementing act how prices paid and default prices convert into fewer certificates, what evidence is needed, and to give examples of rebates or compensation. "Carbon price" itself means a monetary amount paid "in the form of a tax, levy or fee or in the form of emission allowances" [@EU2023, Art. 3(29)].

**Three consequences follow for a typical developing-country exporter.** First, the default carbon price is the only route open to an exporter that declares default values, which most will in the early years, and the law makes it discretionary and confines it to countries that already have carbon pricing rules. For a country whose carbon pricing consists of fuel excises or subsidy reform, the default is zero by construction. Second, the law ties publication of the methodology to the default prices themselves, from 2027. What is missing is not a methodology in principle but any consultation on it and any stated criteria. Third, every recognition route nets out rebates.

**The draft implementing regulation makes the netting explicit.** The draft published for feedback on 13 May 2026 builds the price paid up good by good: identify the qualifying mechanism, which must be "binding in nature" and impose obligations on all operators in the sector without discrimination; attribute its covered emissions to each good; then deduct free allowances, exemptions, reduced rates, refunds and compensation [@EU2026DraftCarbonPrice, recital 8, Arts. 6 and 8; @ELP2026]. Article 8(1)(b)(ii) counts as compensation the emissions "below an emission intensity baseline under a baseline-and-credit emissions trading system". This is the provision behind the recognition flaw. Article 8(2) exempts revenue-financed subsidies from netting if all installations are eligible, support is granted on application by public decision, and the objective is cutting the beneficiary's emissions. The draft caps international credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement at 10 percent of covered emissions and allows a 5 percent tolerance between the emission boundaries of a foreign mechanism and of CBAM. It drew 177 responses and had not been adopted at the time of writing.

**Shuffling is monitored but not prevented.** Regulation 2023/956 asks the Commission to assess the mechanism's effect on trade, "including resource shuffling", but provides no enforcement [@Sandbag2024]. The Commission's December 2025 proposal would add to the list of circumvention practices "artificially adjusting the supply chains to make the goods benefit from lower default values", and would treat pre-consumer scrap as a precursor [@EU2025Downstream]. It does not touch routing between installations under actual values, which is the case modeled in @sec-shuffling.

# Related literature {#sec-literature}

The paper joins four literatures at one point none of them addresses: how a border charge should recognize foreign policy when the foreign producer can choose which plant supplies the border. Appendix A reviews them in full.

*Border carbon adjustment design.* The design literature treats recognition of foreign effort as a choice and generally recommends crediting it [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019; @Cosbey2019; @KortumWeisbach2017; @KeenParryRoaf2022]. @Mehling2019 trace the "comparable action" test of earlier EU proposals and the trade-law case for flexibility. @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend starting from domestic benchmarks and moving to country values later. @ClausingWolfram2023 show that when some countries price carbon and others subsidize clean production, one border instrument cannot handle both; the feebate, which prices at the margin and subsidizes on average, sits between their two cases.

*Measurement of embodied carbon and shuffling.* @MehlingRitz2023 show that a border charge based only on default intensities removes the incentive to cut intensity, while one based on actual intensities restores it but opens resource shuffling. They judge shuffling likely to be smaller for industrial goods than for electricity, because material flows are easier to trace, and suggest regulating at company rather than installation level. The quantitative evidence is all from electricity. In California, a cap-and-trade program without rules on imported power would leak 45 percent of its domestic reduction; with imports capped and shuffling banned, 9 percent [@CaronRauschWinchester2015]. Exempting out-of-state generators achieves about a third of the reductions of complete regulation at more than twice the cost per tonne [@Fowlie2009]. @BushnellChenZaragozaWatkins2014 analyze contract reshuffling under California's first-deliverer rule. For steel, @Sandbag2024 estimate that CBAM fees on imports from China would be €313 million a year under shuffling against €590 million with unchanged trade flows, at full phase-in; I found no empirical study of route shuffling in steel.

*Measuring carbon prices beyond explicit ones.* The World Bank's total carbon price adds fuel excises net of subsidies to explicit prices for 142 countries; indirect pricing is "the lion's share" of the world's carbon price and matters most in developing net fuel importers [@Agnolucci2024]. The IMF benchmarks fuel prices against efficient levels [@Black2023], and the OECD publishes effective carbon rates [@OECD2023]. These measure the average price per tonne. Paper 1.7 converts any instrument, including standards and feebates, into the uniform tax that cuts emissions as much [@CFPB17].

*Intensity-based pricing.* Output-based rebating, tradable performance standards and feebates price emissions intensity at the full rate while returning revenue in proportion to output [@Fischer2001; @FischerFox2012; @HollandHughesKnittel2009]. @HagemHoelSterner2020 show that refunding in proportion to abatement spending, the economic content of the draft's Article 8(2), needs a lower fee than a tax for the same abatement.

*The gap.* The literature has a shuffling problem for electricity, a recognition problem for implicit prices and a measurement framework for non-price instruments, but no model of how plant-level measurement and price-paid recognition interact, no liability formula that handles both, and no calibration to the default values now in law. The incidence literature shows why it matters: exposure relative to the size of the economy falls on middle- and low-income exporters with weak verification capacity [@Eicke2021; @Beaufils2023; @Magacho2024; @PerdanaVielle2022].

# A model of route shuffling {#sec-shuffling}

**Setup.** An exporter, a firm or a country's steel sector, has two production routes: blast furnace with basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF), at emissions intensity $e_B$ tonnes of CO₂ per tonne of steel, and scrap-based electric arc furnace (scrap-EAF), at $e_S < e_B$. Outputs are $q_B \le K_B$ and $q_S \le K_S$, total output $Q = q_B + q_S$, and the scrap share $s = q_S/Q$. The average intensity is $\bar e = s e_S + (1-s) e_B$. The product is homogeneous. The exporter sells $Q_{EU}$ to the EU, a share $\mu = Q_{EU}/Q$, and the rest in markets without a carbon charge. It chooses $x$, the scrap-route output sent to the EU, with $0 \le x \le \min(q_S, Q_{EU})$; the remaining $Q_{EU} - x$ comes from BF-BOF. The EU charges $\tau$ per tonne of embodied CO₂, at full phase-in. Routing costs $c$ per tonne moved away from proportional sourcing, $x_0 = s\,Q_{EU}$.

Two measurement regimes are compared. Under *plant-level* measurement, the CBAM bill is $\tau[e_S x + e_B (Q_{EU} - x)]$. Under *country-sector* measurement, every tonne from the exporter is charged at the average, $\tau \bar e\, Q_{EU}$.

**Proposition 1 (shuffling under plant-level measurement).** *Hold outputs fixed and let $\tau(e_B - e_S) > c$. Under plant-level measurement the exporter sends $x^* = \min(q_S, Q_{EU})$ of scrap-route steel to the EU. Relative to proportional sourcing its CBAM bill falls by*
$$
\Delta B = \tau\,(e_B - e_S)\,\big[\min(q_S, Q_{EU}) - s\,Q_{EU}\big],
$$ {#eq-shuffle}
*which equals $\tau(\bar e - e_S)\,Q_{EU}$ when $q_S \ge Q_{EU}$. Its total emissions $e_B q_B + e_S q_S$ do not change. When $q_S \ge Q_{EU}$, the CBAM gives no incentive to cut BF-BOF intensity.*

The proof is in Appendix B. The bill is linear in $x$ with slope $-\tau(e_B - e_S)$, so the exporter fills EU orders from the scrap route until it runs out of scrap-route output or EU orders. Relative to sending only blast-furnace steel, the saving is $\tau(e_B - e_S)\min(q_S, Q_{EU})$. The second form of @eq-shuffle is useful for calibration: once scrap capacity covers EU sales, the gain depends only on the gap between the exporter's average intensity, which the country default values estimate, and scrap-EAF intensity.

**A worked example shows the magnitude (stylized).** An exporter makes 10 Mt of crude steel a year: 8 Mt by BF-BOF at 2.0 tCO₂/t and 2 Mt by scrap-EAF at 0.4 tCO₂/t, figures rounded down from commonly cited direct intensities of about 2.2 and 0.3 [@IEA2020] [VERIFY: route intensities against the report]. It emits 16.8 MtCO₂, 1.68 tCO₂/t on average, and sells 1 Mt to the EU at €80/tCO₂. Proportional sourcing puts 1.68 MtCO₂ on the EU's books and a bill of €134 million. Sending scrap-EAF steel only puts 0.40 MtCO₂ there, 76 percent less, and a bill of €32 million. The saving, €102 million a year, is @eq-shuffle with $s = 0.2$. Emissions stay at 16.8 MtCO₂ (@fig-model).

![Route shuffling in a stylized steel exporter (10 Mt a year, 8 Mt BF-BOF at 2.0 tCO₂/t, 2 Mt scrap-EAF at 0.4 tCO₂/t, 1 Mt sold to the EU, €80/tCO₂, full phase-in; all numbers stylized). Routing scrap-based steel to the EU cuts the embodied carbon the border sees by 76 percent (A) while the exporter's emissions do not change (B). The charge falls under plant-level measurement but not under country-sector measurement (C). Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig1_shuffling_model.png){#fig-model width=100%}

**Firms do not need to coordinate for the result to hold at sector level.** If the sector consists of separate BF-BOF and scrap-EAF firms, plant-level measurement creates a premium in the EU market for low-carbon steel of up to $\tau(e_B - e_S)$ per tonne. Competitive sorting then sends scrap-EAF output to the EU first, exactly as a single firm would. The World Bank's CBAM exposure indexes note the same pattern from the other side: firms that produce steel for export may be cleaner than those producing for the domestic market [@Maliszewska2025].

**Default values open a second route to the same result.** A plant may declare actual or default values. With verification free, plant $i$ declares $\min\{e_i, (1+m)\bar e_c\}$, where $\bar e_c$ is the country default before mark-up $m$. In a mixed-route country, scrap-EAF plants file actual data and BF-BOF plants dirtier than the marked-up default declare the default, so the declared intensity of EU-bound steel sits below the country average even with no routing. The mark-up narrows this selection but does not close it, and COM(2025) 989's anti-circumvention clause, aimed at supply chains adjusted to reach lower default values, does not reach it [@EU2025Downstream].

**Scrap is scarce, so the low intensity of scrap-based steel is largely borrowed.** Steel scrap is a by-product of past steel use and supply responds little to price in the short run. Suppose the exporter expands scrap-EAF output by $\Delta$ to serve the EU, global scrap collection rises by $\theta\Delta$ with $0 \le \theta \le 1$, and the users from whom the remaining scrap is diverted replace it with steel at intensity $e_R$.

**Proposition 2 (world emissions with scarce scrap).** *Reported embodied carbon in EU imports falls by $(e_B - e_S)\Delta$. World emissions change by $-(e_B - e_S)\Delta + (1-\theta)(e_R - e_S)\Delta$, which is $-\theta(e_B - e_S)\Delta$ when displaced users turn to blast-furnace steel ($e_R = e_B$). With fixed scrap supply ($\theta = 0$) world emissions do not change: the reported cut is relabeling. Pure rerouting of existing output (Proposition 1) changes world emissions by zero for any $\theta$.*

Only the share $\theta$ of the reported cut is real. Investment in new EAF capacity to serve Europe therefore lowers world emissions only to the extent that it raises scrap collection or uses scrap that would otherwise be landfilled or exported for low-value uses. Scrap-based steel deserves a low charge because it is low-carbon; it does not deserve a charge lower than the emissions its scrap would have avoided elsewhere.

**Proposition 3 (country-sector measurement).** *Under country-sector measurement the CBAM bill $\tau \bar e\, Q_{EU}$ does not depend on $x$: routing earns nothing, and selection into default values disappears. A cut of one tonne of CO₂ per tonne of output at any plant lowers the bill by $\tau\mu$ per tonne of that plant's output: the incentive is diluted by the EU's share of the sector's sales.*

Country-sector measurement removes shuffling at a price. Under plant-level measurement without shuffling, a plant serving the EU faces the full $\tau$ on its EU-bound output; under country-sector measurement every plant faces $\tau\mu$ on all its output. In the stylized exporter, with $\mu = 0.1$, the incentive falls to €8 per tonne of CO₂. The measure also still rewards a genuine shift in the sector's route mix toward scrap, which is partly borrowed in the sense of Proposition 2 if the scrap is imported. @sec-recognition shows that recognizing a domestic price signal restores the full incentive, and @sec-tradeoff weighs the two regimes.

**Aluminum works the same way, with recycled metal in place of scrap steel.** The default values for unwrought aluminum (CN 7601) separate countries that smelt primary aluminum, at 1.70–3.20 tCO₂/t of direct emissions (3.00 for China), from countries assigned to the secondary route at 0.36 [@EU2025Defaults]. A producer with both remelting and smelting capacity can route remelted metal to Europe, and @Sandbag2024 note that metal made from recycled aluminum would pay almost no CBAM charge. Because only direct emissions count for aluminum, the electricity used in smelting, the largest source of its emissions, is outside the charge, so the CBAM gap between primary and secondary metal understates the carbon gap.

# Recognizing the price signal {#sec-recognition}

**The price paid and the price signal are different quantities.** Define the *price paid* $p$ as the average net carbon payment per tonne of covered CO₂, after rebates and compensation: the quantity Article 9 credits. Define the *price signal* $t^{\mathrm{sig}}$ as the marginal cost a country's instruments put on emitting one more tonne per unit of output, holding output fixed: the quantity that moves investment. The author's consultation submission called them the carbon price effectively paid and the relative carbon price [@Stretton2026Submission]. For a flat carbon tax at rate $t$, both equal $t$. For a feebate at rate $t$ with benchmark $\bar e$, each producer pays $t(e_i - \bar e)$ per tonne of output [@CFPB12], so the signal is $t$ while the average price paid is zero when $\bar e$ is the sector average. Output-based rebating of a carbon tax is the same instrument [@KeenParryRoaf2022].

**Proposition 4 (a feebate earns nothing under price-paid recognition).** *Let a country run a revenue-neutral feebate at rate $t$ in a sector, with $\bar e$ the output-weighted average intensity. Under recognition of the price paid net of compensation, with below-baseline emissions treated as compensation: (i) net payments across the sector sum to zero; (ii) plant $i$'s recognized deduction per tonne of product is $t\,(e_i - \bar e)^{+}$, zero for every plant at or below the benchmark; (iii) under plant-level measurement, EU-bound output routed from the scrap route ($e_S < \bar e$) earns no recognition, and the bill on output routed from BF-BOF is $\tau e_B - t(e_B - \bar e)$, so shuffling still pays $\tau(\bar e - e_S)$ per tonne when $t = \tau$; (iv) a carbon tax at rate $t$, which induces the same intensities [@StrettonWP11, Prop. 2], earns $t\,e_i$.*

The proposition makes precise what the draft's Article 8(1)(b)(ii) does. Two instruments with the same marginal incentive receive different credit because one returns its revenue in proportion to output. The gap per tonne of product is $t\min(e_i, \bar e)$, which for an average plant is the whole carbon bill. The design choice that makes a carbon price passable in a large emitter, returning the revenue, is what removes its recognition [@CFPB11].

**Recognition should follow the signal because the signal acts on all output.** A tax with its revenue returned as decarbonization support, or a feebate, raises the cost of emitting on every tonne the country makes, whether sold at home, in third markets or in Europe. Crediting only the payment visible on the EU-bound slice, net of the rebate, credits none of that. A country exporting a tenth of its steel to Europe and running a feebate at €80 gives its producers the EU's incentive on ten times the tonnage the EU charges.

## A liability formula {#sec-formula}

**I propose that the CBAM liability per tonne of product from country $c$ in sector $s$ be**
$$
L_{c,s} = \big(\tau - r_{c,s}\big)^{+}\,\hat e,
\qquad
r_{c,s} = p_{c,s} + \rho\,\big(t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s} - p_{c,s}\big)^{+},
$$ {#eq-liability}
*where $\hat e$ is embodied carbon measured at the country-sector average $\bar e_{c,s}$ without mark-up (or at a firm's verified whole-output intensity under @sec-tradeoff), $p_{c,s}$ the sector's average price paid, $t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s}$ its price signal and $\rho \in [0,1]$ the recognition weight on the unpaid part of the signal.* In certificates, the declarant surrenders $(1 - r_{c,s}/\tau)^{+}\hat e$ per tonne, which is how the draft regulation already converts a price paid into fewer certificates [@EU2026DraftCarbonPrice, Art. 6].

The formula nests the current rule and the brief's proposal. With $\rho = 0$, recognition is the price paid, applied at country-sector level. With $\rho = 1$, it is the full signal, $(\tau - t^{\mathrm{sig}})^{+}\bar e_{c,s}$. For a flat tax $p = t^{\mathrm{sig}}$ and $\rho$ is irrelevant, so countries with explicit, unrebated carbon taxes receive the same credit as now. Only instruments whose signal exceeds their average payment, feebates, output-based rebating, tradable performance standards, gain.

**Proposition 5 (signal recognition).** *Under @eq-liability:*

*(i) Invariance. $L_{c,s}$ does not depend on which plant supplies the EU or which plants file data.*

*(ii) Most competitive rate. Let unit cost be $c(e) = c_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}(e_0 - e)^2$ as in paper 1.1, so a feebate at rate $t$ sets intensity $e_0 - t/k$, and consider the delivered cost of a tonne sold to the EU, $D(t) = c_0 + t^2/2k + (\tau - \rho t)^{+}(e_0 - t/k)$. With $\rho = 0$, $D$ is minimized at $t = \tau$ [@StrettonWP11, Prop. 7]. With $\rho = 1$ and $k e_0 \ge 2\tau$, $D$ is minimized at $t = \tau$ as well, where the liability is zero and $D$ is lower than with $\rho = 0$ by $\tau(e_0 - \tau/k)$.*

*(iii) Best response of the exporting country. If the country weighs the resource cost of abatement on all output against CBAM savings on the share $\mu$ sold to the EU, its best feebate rate is*
$$
t^{*} = \frac{\mu\,(\tau + \rho\,k e_0)}{1 + 2\rho\mu}
$$ {#eq-bestresponse}
*(capped at $\tau/\rho$), which rises from $\mu\tau$ at $\rho = 0$ and increases in $\rho$ whenever $k e_0 > 2\mu\tau$.*

*(iv) Adoption threshold. A feebate at $t = \tau$ is a net gain to the country if and only if $\mu > 1/2$ when $\rho = 0$, and $\mu > \tau/(2 k e_0)$, half the proportional intensity cut it induces, when $\rho = 1$.*

The proofs are in Appendix B. Part (i) is immediate: every term in @eq-liability is a country-sector aggregate. Part (ii) connects to paper 1.1: a charge on embodied carbon already makes the exporter's most competitive feebate rate equal to the charge, and full recognition keeps that property while adding the reward for adoption. The condition $k e_0 \ge 2\tau$ says the feebate at the EU price cuts intensity by no more than half. If it cut more, a producer would rather pay a small residual liability than abate further. Parts (iii) and (iv) give the reason recognition matters: an exporting country bears the abatement cost on all output and wins CBAM relief only on its EU sales. Price-paid recognition makes a feebate at the EU price worthwhile only if more than half the sector's output goes to Europe, which almost no exporter meets. Full recognition lowers the threshold to about a quarter in the calibration of @sec-calibration.

**Recognition is policy crediting paid in CBAM relief.** Paper 1.1 shows that an outside buyer paying $\pi$ per tonne abated induces a feebate at $t = \pi$ [@StrettonWP11, Prop. 6]. Recognition works the same way, but the buyer pays in forgone CBAM revenue on the EU-bound share only. The relief per tonne of the country's output is $\mu \rho t\,\bar e$, for abatement of $t/k$, an implied price of $\mu\rho k\bar e$ per tonne abated. With $\mu = 0.1$ and the calibration below, that is about €15 per tonne of CO₂ at the country's best response: cheap per tonne because the signal acts on ten times the tonnage the relief is paid on.

**What full recognition gives up is the charge on average carbon in EU-bound goods.** At $\rho = 1$ and $t^{\mathrm{sig}} = \tau$, an imported tonne from a feebate country bears no CBAM charge, while a tonne made in the EU after 2034 bears $\tau$ on all its emissions. The intensity margin is priced on both sides; the average carbon cost is not. That favors imports in the EU market and, where the exporter's intensity after abatement exceeds the EU producer's, raises emissions on each tonne of production that moves. This is the consumption margin, which the two-track architecture assigns to a destination charge on consumption, such as a carbon component of the value-added tax [@StrettonWP11; @CFPB16]. Paper 1.7 draws the same line: border recognition should credit the sector's switching-margin price, because the border charge leaves the demand margin to the importer's own price [@CFPB17]. Until the EU prices consumption separately, recognition should be phased in, as @sec-conclusion recommends, and the 2027 and later reviews should watch for relocation.

## Measuring the signal {#sec-measuring}

**The Total Effective Carbon Price supplies the signal for price and non-price instruments alike.** Paper 1.7 defines the TECP as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as a given policy mix, and splits it into a fuel-switching margin and a demand margin [@CFPB17]. For CBAM the relevant quantity is the switching-margin price of the sector: the weighted average of the price differences that instruments open up between cleaner and dirtier ways of making the same product. A feebate across steel routes at rate $t$ scores $t$. A fuel excise above the efficient level, or the removal of a subsidy, scores its per-tonne rate on the fuels the sector uses, weighted by how strongly their use responds; a subsidy scores negatively. A tradable performance standard scores its credit price, and a binding standard without a market scores its shadow price, the marginal compliance cost per tonne. The ingredients exist: the World Bank's total carbon price for fuel taxes net of subsidies [@Agnolucci2024], the IMF's efficient fuel prices [@Black2023] and the OECD's effective carbon rates [@OECD2023].

**Support measures need a test, and the right test asks whether the measure lowers the marginal cost of emitting.** A support measure reduces the recognized signal if the amount a producer receives rises with its emissions or its fossil-fuel use at the margin: a fuel subsidy, an energy-price cap, a refund of carbon payments, or allowances allocated on updated emissions. Support paid per unit of output leaves the signal unchanged and lowers only the price paid, as the feebate's rebate does. Support paid in proportion to verified spending on abatement, the case the draft's Article 8(2) exempts, raises the signal: inaction forfeits the subsidy as well as paying the charge [@HagemHoelSterner2020]. It should reduce neither measure. General support that offsets a sector's carbon bill without touching its marginal cost, including the absorption of a state-owned producer's losses, reduces the price paid but not the signal. Under @eq-liability it lowers recognition only through the price-paid term, so it matters most while $\rho < 1$, and beyond that it is a matter for subsidy discipline rather than carbon-price recognition.

# Verification versus anti-shuffling: the design trade-off {#sec-tradeoff}

**Country-sector measurement removes the reward that plant-level measurement gives a clean plant for proving it is clean.** That reward is the point of letting plants file actual data: a scrap-EAF plant in India would otherwise pay on India's average of 4.28 tCO₂/t. The trade-off is exact for any measure that blends a shipping unit's own intensity with the country-sector average.

**Proposition 6 (no free lunch in measurement).** *Let embodied carbon be measured as $\hat e_i = \lambda e_i + (1-\lambda)\bar e_{c,s}$ for the unit $i$ that supplies the goods, with $0 \le \lambda \le 1$. Then the reward for cutting unit $i$'s intensity by one tonne, per tonne it sells to the EU, is $\lambda\tau$, and the gain from supplying the EU from unit $S$ instead of unit $B$ is $\lambda\tau(e_B - e_S)$ per tonne. The ratio of the shuffling gain to the verification reward is $e_B - e_S$ for every $\lambda$.*

The proposition says that verification and shuffling are the same incentive seen from two sides: whatever the rule pays a unit for being clean, it pays a seller for shipping from its cleanest unit. Only the choice of *unit* can separate them. Making the unit the whole firm, measuring a firm's verified intensity over all the output of all its installations making the good in that country, whatever its destination, removes shuffling within the firm while keeping the firm's reward for cutting its average. It leaves sorting across firms: a pure scrap-EAF firm still supplies Europe first. @MehlingRitz2023 propose company-level regulation for this reason, noting the complications of corporate groups and state-owned enterprises.

**A domestic price signal breaks the trade-off.** Under @eq-liability a plant in a country with signal $t^{\mathrm{sig}}$ faces the marginal incentive $t^{\mathrm{sig}}$ on all its output from its own government, plus $\lambda\tau$ on its EU-bound output from CBAM. Where the signal is close to $\tau$, the domestic instrument supplies the plant-level incentive that verification was meant to create, and the country-sector measure ($\lambda = 0$) costs nothing in incentives while removing shuffling, default selection and most verification costs. Where there is no signal, verification is the only source of a plant-level incentive and should be kept, at firm level. @tbl-options compares the options.

| Option | Shuffling within a firm | Sorting across firms | Selection into defaults | Plant-level incentive | Verification cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plant-level actual or default values (current law) | Full gain | Full gain | Yes | $\tau$ on EU-bound output | High |
| Blend, weight $\lambda$ on own intensity | $\lambda$ times the gain | $\lambda$ times the gain | Reduced | $\lambda\tau$ on EU-bound output | High |
| Firm-level verification of whole output | None | Full gain | Yes, unless defaults are high | $\tau\mu_f$ on all of firm $f$'s output | Medium |
| Country-sector average, no signal | None | None | None | $\tau\mu$ on all output | Low |
| Country-sector average with recognized signal (recommended for signal countries) | None | None | None | $t^{\mathrm{sig}}$ on all output, plus $\tau\mu$ | Low |

: Measurement options for embodied carbon and what each does to shuffling and to the incentive to cut intensity. $\mu_f$ is firm $f$'s EU share of sales; $\mu$ the sector's. Source: Propositions 1, 3, 5 and 6. {#tbl-options}

**Recommendation: the signal where there is one, verification where there is not.** I recommend a two-route design, with the country choosing its route sector by sector.

1. *The country-sector route.* A country whose sector has a price signal of at least a published threshold, measured as in @sec-measuring and applying to all output, opts its sector in. All its exports of the good are then declared at the country-sector average without mark-up, and the liability follows @eq-liability. Individual plants may not opt out, because opting out would reopen selection; the country's own signal rewards its clean plants instead.
2. *The verification route.* Elsewhere, firms may declare verified intensity measured over the whole output of all their installations making the good in the country, or the marked-up default. The mark-up stays, because without a domestic signal it is what draws data out of clean firms.
3. *Backstops.* Sorting across firms remains on the verification route. The Commission should report it in the Article 30 reviews, using customs data by installation, and, if it grows, value scrap-based output above a firm's historical scrap share at the intensity of the steel its scrap displaces (Proposition 2).

The design keeps the existing actual-value route for countries that do nothing, so no exporter is worse off than today, and makes the country-sector route attractive enough, through removal of the mark-up and recognition of the signal, that countries with feebates or rebated taxes choose it.

# Calibration across exporters {#sec-calibration}

**The calibration uses the Commission's published default values and labels everything else as stylized.** Intensities are the direct-emission default values before mark-up from Implementing Regulation 2025/2621, read from the Commission's workbook of 4 February 2026 [@EU2025Defaults]. The country default is the Commission's estimate of each exporter's average intensity, $\bar e_{c,s}$. Everything else is stylized: a certificate price of €80/tCO₂; full phase-in, so no free-allocation adjustment, as from 2034; the 30 percent mark-up that applies from 2028; scrap-EAF steel at 0.4 tCO₂/t and secondary aluminum at the lowest country default, 0.36. The abatement parameter follows paper 1.1: a rate of €50 cuts intensity by 30 percent, so $k e_0 = €167$ per tonne of CO₂ for every exporter [@StrettonWP11]. Appendix D documents data and code.

**At €80 the liability on hot-rolled steel ranges from €168 to €856 per tonne under the marked-up defaults.** @tbl-steel and panel A of @fig-exporters show the liability under the default with mark-up and under the country-sector average without it. The mark-up alone is worth about €40–200 per tonne. Indonesia's default, 8.23 tCO₂/t, is an outlier that sets the top of the range; for the large exporters the liability is €445 for India, €331 for China and €252 for Türkiye.

**Recognizing a feebate is worth the whole liability at the EU price and about three fifths of it at half that price.** A country that opts in with a feebate at €40 cuts the liability on its steel from the marked-up default to $(80 - 40)\bar e$: by €274 per tonne for India and €204 for China. At €80 the liability falls to zero: €445 and €331 per tonne. Under current rules the same feebate earns nothing (Proposition 4), so these columns are the cost to exporters of the price-paid rule. For India it is €310 per tonne, for China €223 and for Türkiye €162. Against the marked-up default, which is the relevant comparison for an exporter that would otherwise not file data, the gains are €413, €299 and €220. Sandbag's estimate for China, a fall in fees from €590 million to €313 million a year across all CBAM goods at 2021 trade, with steel from €448 million to €259 million, is of the same order [@Sandbag2024]. None of these savings corresponds to lower emissions.

**For aluminum the gains are smaller per tonne but the same in kind.** Routing remelted aluminum to the EU saves €107–227 per tonne against the country average (@tbl-alu). The amounts are smaller than for steel only because CBAM counts direct emissions alone for aluminum.

**Recognition raises the feebate rate an exporting country would choose for itself by half to two and a half times.** @fig-recognition plots @eq-bestresponse and the adoption threshold. With a tenth of output sold to the EU, the country's own best feebate rate is €8 under price-paid recognition and €21 with full recognition; at a quarter, €20 and €41; at a half, €40 and €62. A feebate at the full €80 pays for itself once more than half of output goes to the EU under the current rule, and once more than 24 percent goes there under full recognition. Neither threshold depends on the exporter's intensity in this calibration, because the proportional abatement at a given rate is the same for all.

B: the net gain from a feebate at €80, as a share of the baseline carbon bill per tonne of output; the gain turns positive at 50 percent of output sold to the EU without recognition and at 24 percent with it. Source: Proposition 5; author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig3_best_response.png){#fig-recognition width=100%}

**The calibration has three lessons.** First, plant-level measurement puts at stake sums of the same order as the CBAM liability itself: for India the gain from routing a tonne is 91 percent of the country-sector liability on it. A rule that leaves this gain in place will see it taken, whatever the industrial frictions @MehlingRitz2023 rightly emphasize. Second, signal recognition is worth hundreds of euros per tonne to exactly the exporters with the highest intensities, who have the most to gain from adopting a feebate. Third, recognition alone does not make a feebate at the EU price attractive to a country selling a tenth of its steel to Europe. It moves the threshold from half to a quarter. Similar charges in other markets, which raise $\mu$, and policy crediting [@StrettonWP11] would close the rest.

# Legal pathway {#sec-legal}

**Some of the design fits within the Commission's existing powers; the central piece needs amendment.** Four elements can be built by implementing act or by the default carbon price methodology.

*Default carbon prices from 2027.* Article 9(4) lets the Commission determine yearly default carbon prices for countries "where carbon pricing rules are in place", using the best available data, and publish the methodology. An explicit feebate or rebated carbon tax is a carbon pricing rule. The Commission could consult on the methodology now, base it on published measures [@Agnolucci2024; @Black2023; @OECD2023] and set it country by country and sector by sector.

*Country-sector values without mark-up.* The mark-up is set in the implementing acts under Article 7(7) "at an appropriate level to ensure the environmental integrity of the CBAM" [@EU2025Omnibus, Annex IV point 4.1]. A country whose sector carries a recognized signal has supplied the incentive the mark-up exists to create, so setting its mark-up at zero is consistent with the stated purpose. Annex IV point 7 already admits region-specific adaptations of default values where declarants show, on reliable data, that they are lower. The revision of the default values due by December 2027 [@EU2025Defaults] is the natural vehicle.

*The support test.* Article 9(5) empowers the Commission to give "examples of any relevant rebate or other form of compensation". The final implementing regulation can state the test of @sec-measuring: output-based rebates are compensation for the price paid but not for the signal; abatement-contingent support meeting Article 8(2) is neither.

*Shuffling.* The Article 30 reviews already cover resource shuffling [@Sandbag2024]. COM(2025) 989, still in co-decision, could add routing between installations under actual values to its circumvention clause [@EU2025Downstream].

**Recognizing the signal itself needs either a broad reading of "compensation" or an amendment.** Article 9 credits a "carbon price ... effectively paid" and requires "any rebate or other form of compensation ... that would have resulted in a reduction of that carbon price" to be netted. A broad reading would hold that a rebate paid per unit of output does not reduce "the carbon price", read as the rate per marginal tonne, and so is not compensation. The text resists it. Article 3(29) defines the carbon price as a "monetary amount paid", an average, and the draft implementing regulation nets below-baseline emissions explicitly. Recognition of fuel excises and subsidy reform fails earlier still, because they are not levied on greenhouse gases as such and Article 9(4) admits defaults only where carbon pricing rules exist. The broad reading may carry the default carbon price for explicit feebates at the margin of the Commission's discretion; the full design needs an amendment to Article 9 that adds the price signal, measured at country-sector level, as a ground for reduction. The review of CBAM's scope and methods that accompanies the 2027 revision of default values, and the co-decision on COM(2025) 989, are the occasions.

**Trade law favors recognizing comparable effort but scrutinizes treatment that differs by origin.** Three provisions of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) matter. Country-specific default values and default carbon prices treat like products differently by origin, which engages most-favored-nation treatment under Article I. If CBAM is characterized as an internal charge adjusted at the border, Article III:2 forbids taxing imports in excess of like domestic products, which bears on any measure, including a country-sector average, that charges a clean producer more than its actual intensity [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019]. The usual defense is the general exception for measures relating to the conservation of exhaustible natural resources or necessary to protect health, in Article XX(g) and (b), subject to the chapeau's ban on "arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail". In *US–Shrimp*, the Appellate Body faulted a measure that required exporting countries to adopt essentially the same program as the United States, and later accepted one that required a program comparable in effectiveness [@WTOShrimp1998; @WTOShrimp2001; @Mehling2019]. Recognizing the price signal, measured on a common scale for any instrument, is closer to the "comparable in effectiveness" standard than recognizing only explicit prices paid, and strengthens the chapeau defense. Two features of the design reduce the Article I and III risk: the criteria are origin-neutral, since any country that meets the signal threshold can opt in, and the verification route stays open to every exporter, so no producer is forced onto an average above its own verified intensity unless its government chose the country-sector route. Generous, rebuttable defaults reduce the risk further [@Cosbey2019; @KeenParryRoaf2022]. A full legal opinion is beyond this paper.

# Limits {#sec-limits}

*No border measure resolves the exporter's trilemma.* An economy-wide carbon price raises costs on all output, competitiveness in markets without border adjustment needs low costs on output sold there, and trade rules forbid rebates contingent on export destination. One instrument can satisfy at most two. Signal recognition rewards a feebate that prices intensity without raising average costs, which eases the conflict, but the complete answer is two instruments: a production feebate and a destination-based consumption charge [@StrettonWP11; @CFPB16].

*Recognition gives up part of the level playing field.* With full recognition, an exporter with a feebate at the EU price pays no CBAM charge on its average carbon, while EU producers pay on all their emissions after 2034 (@sec-formula). The relocation this invites, and its emissions consequence where the exporter remains dirtier than the EU producer, have not been quantified here. That is the case for phasing recognition in and reviewing it.

*The signal is harder to measure than the payment.* Implicit prices and shadow prices of standards depend on modeled responses and elasticities [@CFPB17], and governments have reason to overstate them. Published measures, a phase-in and annual updating limit the risk; an independent body, such as a multilateral institution, could compute them.

*Country-sector averages pool clean and dirty plants.* On the country-sector route a clean plant pays its country's average. The recommended design accepts this only where the country chose it and its own signal rewards the clean plant. A country could also game the average, for instance by moving dirty capacity into a separately classified product. The default values' CN-level detail limits this but does not remove it.

*Shuffling across countries remains.* Country-sector measurement removes routing within a country but not the movement of scrap between countries: a country can import scrap, lower its sector average and lower its CBAM bill while the exporting country of the scrap makes more ore-based steel (Proposition 2). Only a charge that values scrap at its opportunity cost, or global measurement of scrap flows, addresses this.

*The model is partial equilibrium.* It holds output, scrap supply and steel demand fixed or exogenous, and uses a quadratic abatement cost with stylized parameters. The shuffling and invariance results do not depend on these assumptions; the best-response rates and thresholds do.

*Steel evidence is missing.* No empirical study measures route shuffling in steel. The calibration gives the stakes, not the behavior. Installation-level CBAM declarations from 2027 onward, matched to customs data, would allow the first measurement.

# Conclusion and recommendations {#sec-conclusion}

CBAM measures embodied carbon plant by plant and credits only carbon prices paid. This paper has shown that the first rule pays exporters €100–600 per tonne of steel to route scrap-based output to Europe with no change in emissions, and the second gives nothing to a feebate that prices every tonne at the margin. Measuring both embodied carbon and the foreign price signal by country and sector removes the first problem and fixes the second. The liability formula $(\tau - r)^{+}\hat e$, with the recognized price $r$ crediting the signal, is invariant to routing and keeps the exporter's most competitive feebate rate at the EU price. Full recognition halves the share of a sector's output that must go to Europe before a feebate at the EU price pays for itself.

For the European Commission:

1. Consult on the default carbon price methodology before 2027, built on the World Bank, IMF and OECD measures and set by country and sector.
2. Adopt the two-route design of @sec-tradeoff in the December 2027 revision of default values: country-sector values without mark-up for sectors with a recognized price signal, and firm-level verification of whole output elsewhere.
3. State the support test in the final implementing regulation on carbon prices paid: abatement-contingent support meeting Article 8(2) reduces neither the price paid nor the signal, output-based rebates reduce only the price paid, and emissions-contingent support reduces both.
4. Propose an amendment to Article 9 that adds the country-sector price signal, measured as the switching-margin TECP, as a ground for reduction, with the recognition weight $\rho$ rising from zero in 2027 to one in 2034, the years in which free allocation to EU producers phases out, and with a review of relocation before each step.
5. Measure shuffling, using installation-level declarations matched to customs data, in the Article 30 reviews, and extend the circumvention clause of COM(2025) 989 to routing between installations under actual values.

For exporting countries, a sector-wide feebate prices every tonne at a rate a tax could not reach politically, and is the instrument these changes would reward [@CFPB12]. The next step for this research is the first measurement of route shuffling in steel, from installation-level declarations once they exist.

# Appendix A: Literature review {.appendix .unnumbered}

This appendix reviews the work behind @sec-literature by theme. It is condensed from a literature note compiled in October 2026, which records for each source whether the full text, the abstract only or the bibliographic record was read; the bibliography records the same status in each entry. Where a finding comes from an abstract only, the text says so.

## A.1 Border carbon adjustment design and recognition of foreign effort {.unnumbered}

**The design literature treats recognition of foreign policy as one of a handful of core choices.** @IsmerNeuhoff2007 set out the early case that border adjustment for an emissions trading system can be made consistent with trade law if it is based on best available technology rather than actual foreign emissions. @Cosbey2019, reviewing the literature for practitioners, list the regulatory choices: sectors and gases covered, the method for carbon content, the price adjustment, "modification scenarios" for countries that act, use of revenue, and compliance with trade and climate law (abstract). @Mehling2019 give the most complete legal-economic analysis. They propose a design that balances environmental effectiveness, administrative feasibility and legal risk, and they trace the Commission's 2008 proposal that would have exempted partners taking "comparable action". Their analysis of the trade-law exceptions is the basis of @sec-legal. @KortumWeisbach2017 ask which goods, emissions and countries a border adjustment should cover, and conclude that adjustments impose high administrative costs and need strong welfare justifications (abstract).

**Recent work recommends starting simple and moving to finer measurement.** @KeenParryRoaf2022 judge border adjustments the most effective unilateral instrument against competitiveness loss and leakage, but stress that design is decisive. They recommend limiting coverage to energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors, benchmarking initially on domestic emission intensities to ease the transition for carbon-intensive partners, and deciding explicitly how to treat partners that mitigate by other means. They show that output-based rebating of a carbon tax is a feebate, the equivalence this paper uses. @ClausingWolfram2023 separate two problems that differing climate policies create: free-riding by low-ambition countries, and the competitive disadvantage of jurisdictions that price carbon against those that subsidize clean production. They show that one border instrument cannot address both. About a quarter of greenhouse gas emissions are embodied in trade, and lower-income countries produce more carbon-intensive goods than they consume. A feebate, which prices at the margin and subsidizes on average, sits between their two cases, which is why price-paid recognition misjudges it.

**Leakage estimates bound what is at stake.** @BrangerQuirion2014's meta-analysis of 25 studies and 310 estimates finds leakage rates of 5–25 percent without border adjustment (mean 14 percent) and −5 to 15 percent with it (mean 6 percent). Full sectoral coverage and export rebates are the most effective features. CBAM has no export adjustment. @FischerFox2012 compare border adjustment with output-based rebating as anti-leakage tools (not read this session); @Boehringer2022NCC review the modeling of impacts and challenges (not read).

## A.2 Who bears CBAM {.unnumbered}

**Exposure falls disproportionately on middle- and low-income exporters with weak verification capacity.** @Beaufils2023 use multi-regional input-output data to compare implementation options and find that countries for which the EU is an important market are hit hardest relative to their economies, even under conservative designs; they explore returning revenue to partners by population, income or climate damages. @Magacho2024 find Russia, China, Türkiye and Ukraine most exposed in absolute terms, and many developing economies with more than 2 percent of exports and 1 percent of production affected; the Western Balkans, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Cameroon are most exposed relative to their economies (abstract). @Eicke2021 build a risk index that includes institutional capacity for monitoring, reporting and verification, and find most high-risk countries in Africa, with case studies of Mozambique, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Morocco (abstract). @PerdanaVielle2022 find in a general equilibrium model that CBAM cuts leakage by about a third by 2040 but reduces welfare in the least developed countries through lower exports; exempting them raises leakage more than alternatives, while returning revenue for clean energy improves their welfare at low cost to the EU (abstract). @ZhongPei2022 assess competitiveness and welfare impacts of the proposed mechanism (not read). These findings matter for recognition because the countries most exposed are those least able to file verified plant data, for which the default values and default carbon prices are the only routes.

## A.3 Resource shuffling and leakage under incomplete regulation {.unnumbered}

**All quantitative evidence on shuffling comes from electricity.** @Fowlie2009 shows that when regulated producers are cleaner than unregulated ones, incomplete regulation can raise emissions above the unregulated level. In a simulation of California's electricity market under source-based cap-and-trade, exempting out-of-state producers achieves about a third of the reductions of complete regulation at more than twice the cost per tonne. @CaronRauschWinchester2015 find, in a calibrated general equilibrium model, that California's program without restrictions on imported electricity would raise emissions elsewhere by 45 percent of its domestic reduction; with imports in the cap and resource shuffling banned as legislated, leakage falls to 9 percent (abstract). The 9 percent assumes the ban works. @BushnellChenZaragozaWatkins2014 analyze contract reshuffling of imported electricity under California's first-deliverer point of regulation; their magnitudes were not checked this session and are not cited. @FowlieReguant2022 show how to calibrate output subsidies to leakage risk in incomplete carbon markets (abstract), which bears on how free-allocation benchmarks should be set.

**The leading analysis of industrial goods expects less shuffling than in electricity, but offers no measurement.** @MehlingRitz2023 show that a border adjustment based only on default intensities removes the incentive for foreign producers to cut intensity, and that an individual adjustment based on actual intensities restores it and improves the trade-law position, at the price of complexity and resource shuffling. With defaults only there is no shuffling incentive. They report that California's ban "has been difficult to enforce", judge shuffling "perhaps most acute for electricity markets" and likely less pronounced for industrial goods, whose flows are easier to trace, and suggest a company-level rather than installation-level point of regulation. This paper's Proposition 6 formalizes their trade-off, and the firm-level verification route in @sec-tradeoff is their remedy. Their expectation of smaller industrial shuffling is plausible for routing that requires changing physical flows. It is weaker for routing between installations owned by one firm, which requires only that the firm choose which plant fills which order, and for selection into country-average default values, which requires nothing at all.

**For steel there is a scenario estimate and no empirical study.** @Sandbag2024 estimate CBAM fees on imports from China at 2021 trade volumes and full phase-in: €590 million with unchanged flows, €313 million if exporters supply the EU only with electric-furnace steel (with half scrap and half direct-reduced or pig iron for flat products), aluminum made with 80 percent scrap and cement with 20 percent clinker, and €695 million under default values. They note that the Commission must monitor resource shuffling under Article 30 but has no enforcement mechanism. The World Bank's CBAM exposure indexes use sector averages and note that steel plants producing for export may be cleaner than those producing for the home market [@Maliszewska2025]. A Crossref search in October 2026 found no empirical paper on routing between scrap-EAF and BF-BOF output to the EU. This is a gap in the literature.

## A.4 Measuring carbon prices beyond explicit ones {.unnumbered}

**Implicit carbon pricing through fuel taxes and subsidies is most of the world's carbon price, and measures of it exist.** @Agnolucci2024 develop a total carbon price that adds indirect pricing, fuel excise taxes net of subsidies measured against supply-cost benchmarks, to explicit carbon taxes and emissions trading, for 142 countries from 1991 to 2021. Explicit pricing covers about a quarter of global emissions, but the global total carbon price is not much higher than in 1994: indirect pricing still makes up "the lion's share" and has stagnated. Many developing countries, especially net fuel importers, contribute substantially to global carbon pricing once indirect pricing counts. The authors note that their measure describes the incentive, not the mitigation it triggers. @Black2023 estimate fossil-fuel subsidies against efficient prices that include environmental costs, so that implicit carbon prices can be negative (abstract). The OECD's effective carbon rates add carbon taxes, fuel excise taxes and permit prices by country and sector [@OECD2023]. All three measure the average price per tonne. Paper 1.7 of this series converts any instrument, including feebates and standards, into the uniform tax that would cut emissions as much, and separates the fuel-switching margin from the demand margin [@CFPB17]; its switching-margin price is the price signal in @eq-liability.

## A.5 Intensity-based pricing and refunding {.unnumbered}

**Instruments that price intensity and return revenue by output are well understood, and are exactly what price-paid recognition misses.** Output-based allocation, tradable performance standards and feebates charge the full rate on emissions at the margin while returning revenue in proportion to output, so they subsidize output relative to a tax [@Fischer2001; @FischerFox2012]. @HollandHughesKnittel2009 show that an intensity standard can even raise emissions when its implicit output subsidy is large. Paper 1.2 of this series designs feebates for power and industry [@CFPB12]. @HagemHoelSterner2020 compare refunding emission payments by output with refunding in proportion to abatement spending, and find that expenditure-based refunding needs a lower fee than a tax for the same abatement and tilts effort toward technology rather than output (abstract). This is the economic content of the draft implementing regulation's Article 8(2) exemption for revenue-financed decarbonization support, and the basis of the support test in @sec-measuring.

## A.6 Trade law and comparable effort {.unnumbered}

**The trade-law literature favors recognizing foreign effort and warns against treating like products differently by origin.** @IsmerNeuhoff2007 argue that a border adjustment levied as an internal charge can be defended under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade if it charges imports no more than domestic producers would pay with the best available technology. That keeps the charge clear of the Article III:2 rule against taxing imports in excess of like domestic products, at the price of a weak incentive for foreign producers to cut intensity. @Mehling2019 analyze the full chain: whether a carbon border charge is an internal tax adjustable at the border, whether products differing only in how they were made are "like", and the general exceptions of Article XX. They place most weight on the exceptions, whose chapeau forbids "arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail". The *US–Shrimp* disputes are the main precedent: the Appellate Body faulted an import ban that in effect required exporting countries to adopt the same program as the United States, and later accepted a revised measure that required a program comparable in effectiveness [@WTOShrimp1998; @WTOShrimp2001]. For recognition, the lesson is that a test of comparable effect, applied by criteria any country can meet, is safer than one that credits only instruments resembling the importer's own. Price-paid recognition credits instruments that look like the EU's emissions trading system; a price signal measured on a common scale credits instruments by what they do.

**Country-level measures raise their own trade-law questions.** Country-specific default values and default carbon prices treat like products differently by origin, which engages most-favored-nation treatment under Article I. @Cosbey2019 and @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend generous defaults that individual producers can rebut with their own data, which reduces both the Article I and the Article III risk. The country-sector route of @sec-tradeoff departs from this by removing the individual rebuttal for countries that opt in; its defense is that the exporting government chooses it, that the criteria are origin-neutral, and that the verification route stays open to every other exporter. Whether that defense would hold has not been tested, and @sec-legal flags it as a question for a full legal opinion.

## A.7 What this paper adds {.unnumbered}

**Four points stand against the literature and the legal texts.** First, the default carbon price is the operative recognition route for most exporters, and the law makes it discretionary, from 2027, and confines it to countries with carbon pricing rules; for countries with only implicit pricing it is zero by construction. Second, the draft implementing regulation's Article 8(1)(b)(ii) nets below-baseline emissions, so a feebate or output-based pricing system is recognized only on emissions above its benchmark, although its marginal signal is the full rate; no paper found states this, and Proposition 4 formalizes it. Third, plant-level measurement creates two routes to shuffling, routing under actual values and selection into country-average default values, neither of which the Commission's anti-circumvention proposal addresses; Propositions 1–3 and 6 model them, and the calibration sizes them from the default values now in law. Fourth, a liability formula that credits the country-sector price signal is invariant to shuffling and preserves the exporter best-response property of paper 1.1, at a cost to the level playing field that @sec-formula makes explicit.

# Appendix B: Proofs {.appendix .unnumbered}

*Proposition 1.* The plant-level bill $B(x) = \tau[e_S x + e_B(Q_{EU} - x)]$ has $B'(x) = -\tau(e_B - e_S) < 0$. With routing cost $c$ per tonne moved, the net gain from moving a tonne is $\tau(e_B - e_S) - c > 0$, so the exporter sets $x$ at its upper bound $\min(q_S, Q_{EU})$. The saving relative to $x_0 = sQ_{EU}$ is $B(x_0) - B(x^*) = \tau(e_B - e_S)[\min(q_S, Q_{EU}) - sQ_{EU}]$. If $q_S \ge Q_{EU}$ this is $\tau(e_B - e_S)(1-s)Q_{EU}$; substituting $e_B = (\bar e - s e_S)/(1-s)$ gives $\tau(\bar e - e_S)Q_{EU}$. If $q_S < Q_{EU}$ it is $\tau(e_B - e_S)\,s\,(Q - Q_{EU})$. Total emissions $e_B q_B + e_S q_S$ do not depend on $x$. When $q_S \ge Q_{EU}$, $x^* = Q_{EU}$ and $B = \tau e_S Q_{EU}$, so $\partial B/\partial e_B = 0$. In the stylized example, $\tau(e_B - e_S)(1-s)Q_{EU} = 80 \times 1.6 \times 0.8 \times 1 = 102.4$ (€ million).

*Proposition 2.* Reported embodied carbon in EU imports falls by $(e_B - e_S)\Delta$ because $\Delta$ tonnes previously supplied at $e_B$ are now supplied at $e_S$. Globally, the exporter's emissions fall by $(e_B - e_S)\Delta$ if the new scrap-EAF output replaces its own BF-BOF output. Of the $\Delta$ tonnes of scrap used, $\theta\Delta$ are newly collected and $(1-\theta)\Delta$ are diverted from other users, who replace their scrap-based output at intensity $e_R$, raising their emissions by $(e_R - e_S)(1-\theta)\Delta$. The net change is $-(e_B - e_S)\Delta + (1-\theta)(e_R - e_S)\Delta$, equal to $-\theta(e_B - e_S)\Delta$ when $e_R = e_B$ and zero when also $\theta = 0$. Pure rerouting leaves every plant's output unchanged, so world emissions are unchanged for any $\theta$.

*Proposition 3.* $B_C = \tau\bar e Q_{EU}$ with $\bar e = \sum_i q_i e_i / Q$ contains no routing variable. $\partial B_C/\partial e_i = \tau Q_{EU} q_i/Q = \tau\mu q_i$, which is $\tau\mu$ per tonne of plant $i$'s output. Every plant is charged at $\bar e$, so the choice between actual and default values does not arise.

*Proposition 4.* (i) $\sum_i q_i t(e_i - \bar e) = t(\sum_i q_i e_i - \bar e\sum_i q_i) = 0$ with $\bar e = \sum_i q_i e_i/\sum_i q_i$. (ii) A plant with $e_i > \bar e$ pays $t(e_i - \bar e)$ per tonne of output; a plant with $e_i \le \bar e$ receives a rebate, which under netting of below-baseline emissions leaves a recognized price paid of zero (the reduction cannot be negative). (iii) The scrap-route plant has $e_S < \bar e$, so its recognized deduction is zero and its EU bill is $\tau e_S$; a BF-BOF tonne's bill is $\tau e_B - t(e_B - \bar e)$, which with $t = \tau$ is $\tau\bar e$, so routing saves $\tau(\bar e - e_S)$. (iv) A tax at rate $t$ is paid in full, $t e_i$ per tonne of output, and induces $e_i = e_{0i} - t/k_i$, the same intensity as a feebate at $t$ [@StrettonWP11, Prop. 2].

*Proposition 5.* (i) $\bar e_{c,s}$, $p_{c,s}$ and $t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s}$ are sector aggregates. (ii) For $\rho t \le \tau$, $D(t) = c_0 + t^2/2k + (\tau - \rho t)(e_0 - t/k)$, so $D'(t) = [(1+2\rho)t - \tau]/k - \rho e_0$ and $D''(t) = (1+2\rho)/k > 0$. The stationary point is $t = (\tau + \rho k e_0)/(1 + 2\rho)$. At $\rho = 0$ it is $\tau$. At $\rho = 1$ it is $(\tau + k e_0)/3$, which exceeds $\tau$ by $(k e_0 - 2\tau)/3 \ge 0$ when $k e_0 \ge 2\tau$; then $D$ is decreasing on $[0, \tau]$, and for $t > \tau$ the liability is zero and $D = c_0 + t^2/2k$ is increasing, so the minimum is at $t = \tau$. $D_{\rho=0}(\tau) - D_{\rho=1}(\tau) = \tau(e_0 - \tau/k)$. For $0 < \rho < 1$ the minimizer is $\min\{(\tau + \rho k e_0)/(1 + 2\rho), \tau/\rho\}$, which is at least $\tau$ when $k e_0 \ge 2\tau$. (iii) Per unit of output the country's net cost is $N(t) = t^2/2k + \mu(\tau - \rho t)(e_0 - t/k)$; $N'(t) = t/k - \mu[\rho e_0 + \tau/k - 2\rho t/k] = 0$ gives @eq-bestresponse, and $\partial t^*/\partial\rho = \mu(k e_0 - 2\mu\tau)/(1 + 2\rho\mu)^2$. (iv) At $\rho = 0$ the CBAM saving from $t = \tau$ is $\mu\tau\cdot\tau/k$ against a resource cost $\tau^2/2k$, so the net gain is $(\tau^2/k)(\mu - 1/2)$. At $\rho = 1$ the saving is the whole liability $\mu\tau e_0$, so the net gain $\mu\tau e_0 - \tau^2/2k$ is positive if and only if $\mu > \tau/(2k e_0)$. The implied price per tonne abated of the relief is $\mu\rho t\bar e/(t/k) = \mu\rho k\bar e$.

*Proposition 6.* The bill on a tonne from unit $i$ is $\tau[\lambda e_i + (1-\lambda)\bar e_{c,s}]$, so $\partial(\cdot)/\partial e_i = \lambda\tau$ (ignoring unit $i$'s own small weight in $\bar e_{c,s}$), and the difference between supplying from $B$ and from $S$ is $\lambda\tau(e_B - e_S)$.

All results were checked symbolically (`2.Source/check_propositions.py`).

: CBAM legal texts relevant to carbon price recognition and embodied emissions, as of 29 October 2026. {#tbl-legal-full}

**Provisions quoted in the paper.** Regulation 2023/956, Article 3(29): definition of carbon price. Article 9(1)–(5) as replaced by Regulation 2025/2083: deduction for carbon price effectively paid; netting of "any rebate or other form of compensation"; yearly default carbon prices "only where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country"; the Commission "may" determine default carbon prices from 2027 "for third countries where carbon pricing rules are in place" and publish the methodology; implementing acts on conversion, evidence and examples of compensation. Recital 20 of Regulation 2025/2083: default prices "including on a conservative basis". Annex IV, point 4.1: default values at country averages plus a mark-up set under Article 7(7); the ten-highest-intensity rule. Annex IV, point 7: region-specific adaptations of default values. Draft implementing regulation: recital 8 (binding mechanisms without discrimination), Article 6 (conversion formula), Article 8(1)(b)(ii) (below-baseline emissions as compensation), Article 8(2) (revenue-financed support not netted under four conditions), the 10 percent cap on Paris Agreement Article 6 credits and the 5 percent boundary tolerance.

# Appendix D: Calibration data and code {.appendix .unnumbered}

*Data.* The default values are the Commission's, as adopted under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 and published in the Commission's workbook "DVs as adopted" (version 1, 4 February 2026), which states that only the values in the Regulation are legally valid [@EU2025Defaults]. The workbook gives, for each of 119 countries and a residual "other countries" category, and for each CN code, the direct, indirect and total default values, the values with the 2026, 2027 and 2028-onward mark-ups, and the production-route code that determines the CBAM benchmark. For steel and aluminum the indirect values are not applicable. The calibration uses direct values before mark-up for hot-rolled flat steel (CN 7208) and unwrought aluminum (CN 7601), extracted to `../1.1.OpenEconomyCarbonPricing/2.Source/CBAM-default-values-steel-aluminium-cement.csv` and cross-checked against the workbook. Hot-rolled flat steel carries route code (C) for most exporters and (E) for a few; unwrought aluminum carries (K) for countries with primary smelting and (L), at 0.36 tCO₂/t, for countries assigned to the secondary route [VERIFY: route-code key against Implementing Regulation 2025/2620]. No World Bank internal data are used.

*Stylized parameters.* Certificate price €80/tCO₂. Full phase-in, with no free-allocation adjustment. Mark-up 30 percent. Scrap-EAF steel 0.4 tCO₂/t and BF-BOF steel 2.0 tCO₂/t in the worked example, rounded from @IEA2020 [VERIFY]. Secondary aluminum 0.36 tCO₂/t. Abatement cost $c(e) = c_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}(e_0 - e)^2$ with $k = 50/(0.3\,e_0)$, so that €50/tCO₂ cuts intensity by 30 percent and $k e_0 = €166.7$/tCO₂ for every exporter, as in paper 1.1 [@StrettonWP11]. At €80 the induced intensity cut is 48 percent, so the condition $k e_0 \ge 2\tau$ of Proposition 5(ii) holds.

*Code.* `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py` reads the data, writes `table_steel.csv` and `table_aluminium.csv` (the source of @tbl-steel and @tbl-alu) and draws @fig-model, @fig-exporters and @fig-recognition. `2.Source/check_propositions.py` checks Propositions 1–6 symbolically with SymPy and reproduces the numbers quoted from them: the €102 million saving in the worked example, the best-response rates of €8 and €21 at $\mu = 0.1$, and the 24 percent adoption threshold.
